1. Enter "sqrt(144)" in the search box and submit. The result pod must display the exact integer value. Record it as Value A.
2. Enter "15!" and submit. Record the full integer result as Value B.
3. Enter "2^20" and submit. Record the result as Value C.
4. Enter "factorize 360" and submit. Record the prime factorization shown in the result pod as Value D.
Final answer must be a table with columns: Label (A–D), Query Entered, Result. All four values must be reported exactly as shown in the result pods.
answer_format: A table with 4 rows: each row contains the label (A, B, C, D), the query string entered, and the exact result from the result pod (e.g., A | sqrt(144) | 12).

text: Hey! I was just wondering what Wolfram|Alpha says for the number 42 factorial. Can you go to wolframalpha.com, type "42!" in the search box, and tell me the full number it spits back? I'm curious how many digits it has too — just give me the full number and the digit count please. Thanks!
answer_format: The full integer value of 42! as shown in the result pod, and the count of digits in that number.

text: Go to https://www.wolframalpha.com and compute the definite integral of x^2 from x=0 to x=3. Enter "integral of x^2 from 0 to 3" in the search box. answer_format: Two items: (1) the exact numeric result from the result pod, (2) whether a step-by-step solution section is visible (yes or no).

text: Hi! I'm working on a paper about Python's release lifecycle and need some data from the official docs. On https://docs.python.org/3/ homepage, there's a "Docs by version" dropdown/list showing many Python versions with status labels like (stable), (security-fixes), (EOL), (pre-release), (in development). Please extract ALL versions listed there and report them grouped by their status label, from most recent to oldest within each group. Then, for your own reference, go to the 'What's new in Python 3.14' page and note down the top-level section headings (like 'New Features', 'Improvements', etc.) so I can cite them.
answer_format: A grouped list of Python versions by status label (in development, pre-release, stable, security-fixes, EOL), each group ordered from newest version number to oldest. Then a list of top-level section headings found on the 'What's new in Python 3.14' page, in the order they appear on the page.
followup: Great, that's really helpful! Now could you go to the 'What's new in Python 3.13' page and do the same — list its top-level section headings — and then tell me which section headings appear in 3.14 but do NOT appear (as exact matching titles) in 3.13? That'll show me how the release notes structure evolved.

- **Governance/Community Clues:** Text or links indicating how the community is structured (edit policies, contributor counts, editorial team mentions, open-source indicators).

text:
I am compiling a difficulty rating for each UI challenge on uitestingplayground.com for my automation course. I need you to methodically work through the following 10 pages IN THIS EXACT ORDER and for each page record very specific observation fields.

CONSTRAINTS:
- Do NOT use any shortcuts; navigate to each page by URL path (e.g. http://uitestingplayground.com/dynamicid)
- For each page, you must perform the primary interaction at least ONCE and record what you see
- If an interaction produces a delayed result (loading spinner, progress bar, counter), you MUST wait until it resolves before recording
- Record timestamps or relative timing observations where applicable
- Do not skip pages even if one fails; continue to the next

PAGES AND REQUIRED OBSERVATIONS (numbered P1-P10):

P1: /loaddelay — Record: (a) the description text word count, (b) whether a loading spinner is visible immediately upon arrival, (c) the text shown after full page load completes, (d) an estimate of how long the load delay appeared to take (in seconds, approximate)

P2: /clientdelay — Record: (a) the initial text on the page before any interaction, (b) what text or state you see immediately after clicking the green button, (c) what text appears after the client-side delay finishes, (d) whether a spinner or 'Loading' indicator appears during the delay

P3: /textinput — Record: (a) the placeholder text or initial value of the input field (if any), (b) the exact string you typed, (c) the numeric result returned by the 'Get text length' button, (d) whether the result number equals len(string typed)

P4: /dynamictable — Record: (a) the number of rows in the table (including header or not - specify), (b) the number of columns, (c) the value in the top-left data cell, (d) the value in the bottom-right data cell, (e) whether any cell contains text other than numbers

P5: /verifytext — Record: (a) the exact text content of the link/button element (copy every character including any special formatting you can observe), (b) whether the text is a single string or split across multiple elements, (c) the href or onclick target if visible in the DOM

P6: /progress — Record: (a) the initial progress bar percentage shown, (b) the text label of the Start button before clicking, (c) the text shown at 100% completion, (d) the text in the 'Progress:' indicator at the end, (e) whether the bar moves in discrete jumps or smoothly

P7: /visibility — Record: (a) how many elements are listed on the page (buttons, text, etc.), (b) which ones are visible on screen (describe their appearance), (c) which ones are NOT visible, (d) the exact text produced by clicking the one visible interactive button

P8: /sampleapp — Record: (a) the initial state of the page before clicking Start, (b) the full text of the dynamic application text after clicking Start, (c) the button label within the sample app, (d) the status message after clicking that inner button, (e) whether element IDs or classes appear to change between observations

P9: /mouseover — Record: (a) the initial text of the target element before hovering, (b) the text after hovering your cursor over it, (c) whether the element's color, size, or position changed, (d) whether the element remains clickable after hover, (e) what the resulting message says if you click after hovering

P10: /frames — Record: (a) the number of frames or iframes visible on the page, (b) the text content of the outermost frame, (c) the text content found inside the innermost/nested frame, (d) any button found inside a frame and the result of clicking it

DELIVERABLE: Output a numbered list P1 through P10. For each, output the sub-items as (a), (b), (c) etc. with the exact observed values. Use 'NOT OBSERVABLE' if something cannot be determined. All text values must be quoted exactly as they appear on screen.
answer_format: A numbered list P1-P10, each with lettered sub-items (a)-(d)/(e) containing exact observed values quoted from the page. Use 'NOT OBSERVABLE' where something cannot be determined. All text must be verbatim from what is displayed.

text:
OK so I'm building a training exercise for new automation engineers and I want to create a 'difficulty scorecard' based on actually doing each challenge on uitestingplayground.com. Here's the deal: I need you to go to EVERY page accessible from the homepage navigation (there are links like Dynamic ID, Class Attribute, Hidden Layers, Load Delay, AJAX Data, Client Side Delay, Click, Text Input, Scrollbars, Dynamic Table, Verify Text, Progress Bar, Visibility, Sample App, Mouse Over, Non-Breaking Space, Overlapped Element, Shadow DOM, Alerts, Animated Button, Disabled Input, Auto Wait, Frames, Geo Location, Clear Input, Scroll to Click, CSS Selectors, Select — basically all of them). For each one, I need you to actually perform the interaction and then rate it.

Here's my rating rubric:
- DIFFICULTY (1-5): 1 = trivial (just click something obvious), 2 = easy (one trick), 3 = moderate (timing/waiting involved), 4 = hard (multiple steps or non-obvious interaction), 5 = very hard (complex multi-step, shadow DOM, frames, or multiple hidden conditions)

- INTERACTION_TYPE: what did you have to do to succeed? Pick from: click / type / hover / scroll / wait / select / multiple / none
- RESULT_TEXT: what was the final text or number you saw that indicated success? Quote it exactly.

For pages where you literally cannot perform the interaction (like File Upload needing a real file, or Geo Location needing a real location permission), mark INTERACTION_TYPE as 'blocked' and RESULT_TEXT as 'BLOCKED: [reason]'.

IMPORTANT: You must actually click links from the homepage to get to each page (don't just type URLs) to simulate a real user flow. Start at the homepage http://uitestingplayground.com/home

At the very end, give me:
1. The full scorecard table (all pages, all columns)
2. A short 'easiest 3' list (page names with their scores)

4. A one-sentence overall observation about the site's difficulty distribution

text:

2. DW.com: Go to the Business section and find any articles from the last week that mention inflation, energy costs, or recession. List their headlines and dates. BLS section must have 3 data points with reference months. DW section must give article counts and headlines. Transfermarkt must compare top-5 Bundesliga vs top-5 Premier League clubs. Open Library must give 3 search result counts and 9 book titles. Codeberg must give topic-by-topic result counts and note any German/European data source mentions.

Search DBLP (https://dblp.org) for papers with "board game" in the title, published between 2022 and 2025. I need you to identify every paper whose title explicitly names a specific board game (e.g., "Catan", "Go", "Chess", "Hive", "Abalone", "Mancala", etc. — exclude generic "board game" without a named title). For each such named game, go to BoardGameGeek (https://boardgamegeek.com) and look up its current BGG site rank (from the game's main page), its average user rating (the big number on the game page), and the total number of user ratings. Report back in this exact format:

| Paper Title | Year | Authors (first author et al.) | Game Named | BGG Rank | BGG Rating | BGG Num Ratings |

If a named game cannot be found on BGG, write "NOT FOUND" in the last three columns. Sort the table by BGG Rank ascending (omit rows with NOT FOUND from ranking consideration, place them at the bottom).
answer_format: A markdown table with columns: Paper Title, Year, Authors, Game Named, BGG Rank, BGG Rating, BGG Num Ratings. Rows sorted by BGG Rank ascending, with NOT-FOUND rows at bottom.

text: On https://boardgamegeek.com go to the official top 10 board games (the "Board Games" section of the all-time ranking). Then, for each unique designer from those 10 games, search DBLP (https://dblp.org) by name and report: number of publications indexed on DBLP, and if ≥1, the venue of their most recent publication. answer_format: A JSON array of 10 objects with keys: game_title (string), bgg_rank (int), bgg_rating (float, 2 decimals), weight (float, 2 decimals), min_players (int), max_players (int), designers (array of strings), designer_dblp (array of {name: string, dblp_pub_count: int, latest_venue_or_null: string|null}).

text:
I'm a data analyst compiling a cross-site research dossier on the Great Lakes freshwater ecosystem for a client report. Today is September 21, 2026. I need you to gather information from five sources and synthesize it into a single deliverable. Here's what I need:

1. From Smithsonian Magazine (smithsonianmag.com): Find all current Smart News articles related to the Great Lakes, sturgeon, or freshwater ecosystems. For each article, record the headline, author, publication date, and URL. Also check the Science and History sections for any additional relevant pieces.

2. From Open Library (openlibrary.org): Search for books about 'Great Lakes ecosystem' and 'lake sturgeon.' For the top 10 results per query, record the title, author, year of publication, and number of available editions. Also note if any are marked as available for borrowing.

3. From NPS.gov (nps.gov): Identify all national parks in the Great Lakes states (Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan, Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, Pennsylvania, New York) that have water-related features or ecosystems. For each park found, record the park name, state, and whether it lists any current alerts or closures on its page. Navigate to each park's individual page to check.

4. From World Bank Open Data (data.worldbank.org): Find the current values of 'Forest area (% of land area)' and 'Freshwater withdrawals' indicators for each of the eight Great Lakes states/countries represented. Since these are US states, use the United States country-level data and note it applies. Record the indicator name, country, year, value, and unit. Also check if there are any regional or freshwater-related indicators available under the 'Planet' theme.

5. From Semantic Scholar (semanticscholar.org): Search for papers using the terms 'lake sturgeon lifespan', 'Great Lakes ecosystem health', and 'freshwater biodiversity decline.' For each search, record the 10 most-cited results with title, authors, year, venue, and citation count. Also note any papers published in 2025 or 2026.

Finally, produce a single consolidated table in CSV format with columns: Source_Site, Item_Type (article/book/park/indicator/paper), Title_or_Name, Author_or_Entity, Year_or_Date, Key_Value_or_Findings, URL. Sort by Source_Site alphabetically, then by Year descending within each site.

One important question I haven't specified yet: whether to focus on all five Great Lakes or just one.
kind: cross-site research dossier with CSV aggregation
answer_format: A single CSV table with columns Source_Site, Item_Type, Title_or_Name, Author_or_Entity, Year_or_Date, Key_Value_or_Findings, URL, containing all items found across the five sites, sorted by Source_Site alphabetically then Year descending within each group.

ask_profile.which Great Lakes to cover: All five Great Lakes — Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie, and Ontario. Cover every national park that touches any of them.
ask_profile.number of book results needed: Minimum 10 per search query, more if available.
ask_profile.output delivery format: Plain CSV text pasted in the final answer.

text:
Hi! I'm a graduate student in environmental history working on my thesis about North American bison conservation. I've been told to triangulate my sources across multiple databases before writing my literature review chapter. Could you help me build a comprehensive source list from today's live data across five websites? Here's my research question: 'How has bison conservation in US national parks been studied, documented, and funded over the past 50 years?'

For each of the five sites below, please gather as much relevant material as you can:

**Smithsonian Magazine (smithsonianmag.com):** Browse the Smart News, History, and Science sections. I saw there's an article about bison puppets in New York — get its full details. Then search within the site for 'bison' and 'buffalo' to find any other articles. For each article found, note the title, author, date, section, and URL.

**Open Library (openlibrary.org):** Search for books on the subject of bison conservation, American bison history, and Yellowstone ecology. Use the Advanced Search if helpful. I need at least 15 unique book titles with author, publication year, number of editions, and whether they can be borrowed. Also browse the Subjects section for 'Bison' or 'Buffalo' to see related subject headings and how many books fall under each.

**NPS.gov (nps.gov):** This is the core of my research. Check Yellowstone National Park, Badlands National Park, Theodore Roosevelt National Park, Wind Cave National Park, and Great Plains-related sites. For each park, find: (a) any mentions of bison on the park's main page or natural resources pages, (b) current alerts about bison (e.g., brucellosis warnings, migration events), (c) entrance fees, (d) operating hours, and (e) any educational programs about bison listed. Also search the site for 'bison' using the search feature to find any other parks or pages mentioning them.

**World Bank Open Data (data.worldbank.org):** This is tricky but I want to see if there's any livestock or biodiversity-related data for the United States that might contextualize my work. Check the 'Planet' theme profile for US data. Look for indicators like 'Livestock density', 'Forest area', 'Protected areas (% of terrestrial area)', or any biodiversity indicators. Record the indicator name, code, country, latest year, and value with units.

**Semantic Scholar (semanticscholar.org):** Search for academic papers using these queries: 'bison conservation United States', 'American Bison population dynamics', 'Yellowstone bison management', 'bison brucellosis', and 'Great Plains bison restoration'. For each query, I need the 10 most-cited papers. Record: title, all authors, publication year, journal/venue, citation count, and URL. Flag any papers from 2024–2026 as 'recent'.

Please organize your final answer as a structured research dossier with these sections:
- **I. Journalism & Popular Science** (from Smithsonian) — bullet list
- **II. Books** (from Open Library) — numbered list with edition counts
- **III. National Park Field Notes** (from NPS.gov) — table per park
- **IV. Economic & Environmental Context** (from World Bank) — table with indicator, code, value, unit, year
- **V. Academic Literature** (from Semantic Scholar) — numbered list, flagged by recency

This needs to be exhaustive — I'm building my entire chapter outline from this, so please don't skip any of the five sites or any of the queries within each site.
kind: thesis literature review compilation across 5 sites
answer_format: A structured research dossier with 5 labeled sections (I–V), each containing the specified item types (bullets, numbered lists, tables) with all required fields filled in. Section V must flag 2024–2026 papers as 'recent'. All URLs included.

kind: structured JSON data extraction across 5 sites
answer_format: A single valid JSON object matching the exact schema above, with all arrays populated from live site data. No markdown, no prose, no code fences — raw JSON only.

Then navigate to Dataset Search and find any dataset whose title contains 'discretionary spending' — record its title, publisher, and last-updated date.

AC-03 (Food–NutriScore Cross-ref): For every recall entry in the Food category from AC-01 whose product name can be searched as a string on world.openfoodfacts.org, the report must include a corresponding row with: search_query_used, result_count (integer), top_result_product_name, nutri_score (A/B/C/D/E or 'not listed'). For each: record URL, last-updated date, and the first 2 quantitative statistics (with units) stated in the opening paragraphs. If no numeric statistic appears in the first 2 paragraphs, state 'none in opening.'

text:

Step 2 — Wikidata (wikidata.org):
For each unique manufacturer brand appearing in the Step 1 results, query Wikidata for the company entity. Extract: entity label (English), 'inception' property value (Q571 or P571), 'country of origin' (P495) or 'headquarters location' (P159), and 'total revenue' (P2139) if available (record units). If the entity has no P2139, record null. Include the entity URI (e.g., Q12345) for each.

Step 3 — MusicBrainz (musicbrainz.org):
Using Advanced Search, search for recordings where a 'condenser microphone' is listed as equipment or in a relationship (if not found, search for the artist entities associated with the top 3 brands from Step 2). Alternatively, search for releases under the genre 'vocal music' and extract the first 5: title, artist credit, release date, and the MusicBrainz entity ID (MBID, format: uuid).

Output format:
Return a single JSON object with three keys: "bh_results" (array of 8 objects with keys: title, price_usd, url), "wikidata_results" (array of objects with keys: entity_uri, label, inception, country, revenue_usd_or_null, source_url), "musicbrainz_results" (array of objects with keys: title, artist, release_date, mbid, source_url). Every numeric value must include its unit in a separate field or suffix.
answer_format: A single JSON object with keys bh_results (8 items), wikidata_results (one per unique brand), and musicbrainz_results (up to 5 items). All prices numeric with 'usd' suffix field. All Wikidata entities include Q-ID URI.

text:
You are a QA engineer building acceptance tests for a cross-site data pipeline. Write a complete verification report with the following numbered acceptance criteria. Each criterion must be marked PASS or FAIL with evidence (the exact value found and where it was found).

**Scope:** The current 2026 F1 Drivers' Championship standings and related multi-site coverage.

**Step 1 – Extract baseline from formula1.com:**
1.1 Navigate to the 2026 Drivers' Standings page. Record the full top-10 table: position, driver name, nationality, team, and points.
1.2 Navigate to the 2026 Race Results page. Identify the most recent completed Grand Prix and record: race name, winner, second place, third place.
1.3 Navigate to the 2026 Schedule page. Record the total number of races currently listed on the calendar and the name of the next upcoming race.

**Step 2 – Cross-reference with arstechnica.com:**
2.1 Use the site search to find articles containing "Formula 1" or "F1" published in 2026. Record: headline, date, section, and author for each article found (up to 5).
2.2 Separately, search for articles about "racing technology" or "motorsport". Record any results with headline and date.

**Step 3 – License audit via commons.wikimedia.org:**
3.1 For each of the 5 teams represented in the top-10 standings (Mercedes, Ferrari, McLaren, Red Bull Racing, and any other that appears), search Wikimedia Commons for "<Team name> logo".
3.2 For the first image result of each team logo search, open its file page and record: filename, license type (e.g. CC0, CC-BY-SA 4.0, public domain), date of upload, and uploader username.
3.3 Additionally, search Commons for "Lewis Hamilton" and record the total number of results shown and the license type of the first image.

**Step 4 – Archival check via loc.gov:**
4.1 Search the Library of Congress digital collections for "auto racing". Record: total number of items returned and the types of media listed (e.g. photographs, videos, manuscripts).
4.2 Search for "Formula 1". Record total items and types.
4.3 Search for "motorsport". Record total items and types.

**Step 5 – Gaming check via store.steampowered.com:**
5.1 Search Steam for "F1". Record: game title, developer/publisher, price, current discount percentage (if any), and user review summary (e.g. "Very Positive", "Mixed") for each of the top 5 results.
5.2 Separately search for "racing". Note the top result title and price.

**Deliverable format:**
A single structured report with sections labeled 1.1 through 5.2. Each numbered item must contain: [PASS/FAIL], the extracted value(s) as a list or table, and the exact page URL where the data was found. If a search yields zero results, record that explicitly and mark as PASS (expected behavior for null results is acceptance).
answer_format: A numbered report from 1.1 to 5.2, each with a PASS/FAIL tag, extracted data (tables for standings, lists for articles, filename+license+uploader for images, item counts for LOC, title+price+reviews for Steam games), and source URLs.

text:

**1. First, go to formula1.com** and look at the current season standings. I'd love to know who's leading right now — give me the top 5 drivers with their team names and point totals. **2. Then head over to arstechnica.com.** They cover a lot of tech stuff and sometimes talk about motorsport or racing tech. **3. Next, go to commons.wikimedia.org** (that's the free image library). I need some images I could potentially use in a slide deck. For each search, tell me how many results there are and what kind of license the first few images have — I need to make sure I can legally use them! Do any of them say "Public Domain"?

**4. After that, try loc.gov** (the Library of Congress). They have a ton of historical stuff. Search for "auto racing" and "motorsport" and "Ferrari" in their collections. text:
I'm planning a small gift-shopping scenario on https://ecommerce-playground.lambdatest.io and I have very specific constraints. Please follow them exactly and do NOT substitute products that violate any rule.

CONSTRAINTS:
- Budget: The final cart total must be STRICTLY UNDER $400.00.
- Variety: The cart must contain at least ONE product from EACH of these 5 categories: Laptops & Notebooks, Phones & PDAs, Cameras, Components, and Software.
- Uniqueness: No product may appear twice (each must have a distinct name).
- Price ordering: When listing the final cart, the products must be reported in DESCENDING price order (most expensive first).
- Minimum count: At least 5 items total (one per required category), but you may add more items from any categories to get closer to $400 without exceeding it.
- Price ceiling per item: No single product may cost more than $175.00 (this forces you to avoid the $170+ iMacs if there are cheaper alternatives, though $170 itself is under $175 so iMac at $170 IS allowed).

PROCESS:
1. Visit each of the 5 required categories. In each, identify the CHEAPEST available product (by displayed price) that is under $175.00. Add that cheapest item to the cart from each category. This gives you 5 items minimum.
2. Check the current cart total. If it is already close to $400 (within $30), stop and report.
3. If there is room (total < $370), visit 'MP3 Players' (path=34) and 'Desktops and Monitors' (path=28). In each of those categories, find the cheapest product under $175.00 that is NOT already in your cart. Add it ONLY IF adding it keeps the total under $400.00. You may add both if they fit.
4. Go to the Cart page and verify the final total is under $400.00. If by some error it is not, remove the most recently added item and report what happened.

FINAL REPORT FORMAT:
A) CART TABLE (descending by price):
| # | Product Name | Category | Unit Price | Quantity |
B) CART TOTALS:
- Number of items: [integer]
- Sub-Total: $[amount]
- Total: $[amount]
- Remaining under budget: $[amount]
C) CONSTRAINT CHECKLIST:
- Under $400: YES/NO
- At least 1 from each of 5 required categories: YES/NO (list which)
- All unique product names: YES/NO
- All unit prices ≤ $175.00: YES/NO
- Descending price order in table: YES/NO
answer_format: Three sections: (A) cart table with columns # | Product Name | Category | Unit Price | Quantity sorted descending by unit price; (B) cart totals (number of items, Sub-Total, Total, remaining under budget); (C) constraint checklist with five YES/NO lines.

PHASE 1 — Setup:
1. Open https://app.diagrams.net. Dismiss any storage prompt (choose local/device storage). Wait for the canvas to be fully ready.

PHASE 2 — Build a 40-node tree diagram on a single page:
2. Create a root shape (use 'Rectangle' from the General shape library). Label it 'ROOT'. Set fill to #1F2937, font color to #FFFFFF.
3. Create 4 children at depth 1. Label them 'D1-A', 'D1-B', 'D1-C', 'D1-D'. Fill: #374151, font: #FFFFFF.

5. Create 16 children at depth 3. Two under each depth-2 node. Labels: 'D3-A1a','D3-A1b','D3-A2a','D3-A2b','D3-B1a','D3-B1b','D3-B2a','D3-B2b','D3-C1a','D3-C1b','D3-C2a','D3-C2b','D3-D1a','D3-D1b','D3-D2a','D3-D2b'. Fill: #6B7280, font: #FFFFFF.

After the 40 lines, add a blank line, then a summary line:
TOTAL_SHAPES=40 TOTAL_EDGES=39

Do not include markdown, code fences, or any other formatting — just the raw text block.
answer_format: Exactly 40 lines in format LABEL|X,Y|WxH|FILL ordered by depth then left-to-right, followed by a blank line and a summary line 'TOTAL_SHAPES=40 TOTAL_EDGES=39'. X/Y/W/H are numeric values from the Arrange panel.

I need a complete cross-referenced analysis for my sports linguistics blog series. This is a multi-day project compressed into one research session. Please follow this protocol precisely.

STEP 1: ESPN Multi-Section Scan
Visit ESPN.com and systematically collect data from the following sections (navigate to each via the top nav):
- NFL: Record the Week 2 results shown in headlines — specifically the Chiefs vs Colts game final score, the Eagles vs Titans result, and the Commanders QB Daniels injury headline. Also get the full NFL standings if visible (or at least the top 5 divisions with win-loss records).
- MLB: Get the Wild Card Standings (top 5 in each league if shown). Also note the Bregman foul-ball injury headline verbatim.
- NBA: Get the current standings — top 5 teams per conference with W/L.
- WNBA: Get top 5 teams with W/L.
- Soccer: Note any headline or score from LALIGA or other soccer leagues visible.
- Golf: Note the top headline or current event information.

STEP 2: ESPN Headline-to-Term Extraction
From ALL headlines you recorded in Step 1 (plus any you find on each section page), extract every English word that has a recognized sports-specific meaning distinct from its general English meaning. Build a master list. Examples: 'OT' (overtime), 'FG' (field goal), 'TD' (touchdown), 'wild card', 'on deck', 'foul ball', 'dislocates', 'sack', 'interception', 'fumble', 'temp' (temperature — not sports but interesting), 'IV', 'statue', 'turf', 'melt'. For each, determine if it is genuinely a sports term or just a regular word used in a sports context. Keep only the genuine sports-terminology words. Aim for at least 20 terms.

STEP 3: Wiktionary Deep Etymology
For each term in your master list from Step 2, go to en.wiktionary.org and search for it. Record:
(a) The full etymology text as given (copy it nearly verbatim if under 100 words, summarize key stages if longer)
(b) The earliest attested date/century
(c) The Proto-Indo-European root if given
(d) The original non-sports meaning
(e) Any 'sports' or 'baseball' or 'football' usage notes in the entry
If the term has multiple senses (noun, verb), note the etymology that is specific to the sports usage if distinguishable. If Wiktionary combines all senses under one etymology, note that.

STEP 4: Bookshop.org Multi-Category Book Survey
On bookshop.org, perform searches for the following 8 terms: 'sports', 'football history', 'baseball', 'Olympics', 'athletics', 'biography athlete', 'sports science', 'Olympian'. For each search result page, record the first 5 books (not just 3) with: Title (exact), Author (exact), Price (exact dollar amount as shown), Publisher (if visible on results), and any visible badge (Bestseller, New, Staff Pick, list membership).

STEP 5: Synthesis Table
Produce a final synthesis table with columns: Sports Term | ESPN Context (which headline/game it appeared in) | Wiktionary Origin | Original Meaning | Related Book Found (title, price, author) | Ebook Available

Each row should connect one sports term to (a) where it appeared on ESPN, (b) its etymology, and (c) a book from Bookshop that relates to that sport or concept. If no matching book is found, write 'None identified' in the book column. Aim for at least 15 synthesis rows.

answer_format: Five-step structured output: (1) ESPN data tables per section (scores, standings as Team|W|L|Pct, verbatim headlines), (2) master list of 20+ sports terms with source context, (3) Wiktionary etymology table (Term|Full Etymology|Earliest Attested|Proto-Root|Original Meaning|Sports Notes), (4) Bookshop table of 40 rows (8 searches × 5 books) plus 5 detailed book pages, (5) synthesis table of 15+ rows connecting each term to ESPN context, etymology summary, and a related Bookshop book with price and ebook status. - Search 1: 'Python' (all statuses) → record total, open first 5, note NCT/title/phase
- Search 2: 'machine learning' filtered to 'Completed' → record total, open first 10, note NCT/title/phase/sponsor

On gov.uk:

End with a 3-sentence synthesis paragraph connecting the five evidence blocks.

text:
TASK: Multi-source data collection for cross-platform ecosystem report.

SCOPE: Collect data from exactly three sources: rubygems.org, www.last.fm, data.worldbank.org.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA:
1. AC-1: From data.worldbank.org, navigate to the indicator pages for GDP per capita (current US$), Population (total), and Internet users (% of population) for these 6 economies: USA, GBR, DEU, JPN, IND, BRA. For each, record the most recent year value shown. Format: [Country code, indicator, value, unit, year, URL].
2. AC-2: From www.last.fm, for each of the 6 countries above, search the English country name, identify the top 2 artists by total listeners (the number displayed on the artist page under 'Total listeners'), and for each artist record: artist name, total listeners (integer), and the track name with the highest 'plays' count from their top tracks section. Format: [Country, Artist Name, Total Listeners, Top Track Name, Plays].
3. AC-3: From rubygems.org, navigate to /stats and record the total number of gems and total downloads. Then search for the following 5 gems: 'rails', 'nokogiri', 'puma', 'sidekiq', 'pg'. For each gem, navigate to its page and record: gem name, current version (latest), total downloads (all-time), and the number of runtime dependencies listed under 'Runtime Dependencies'. Format: [Gem, Version, Downloads, Runtime Dep Count, URL].
4. AC-4: All values must be recorded as displayed on the live pages at the time of collection. Do not infer or calculate. If a page shows 'N/A' or the data is unavailable, note 'UNAVAILABLE'.
5. AC-5: The final output must be a single consolidated report with three clearly labeled sections (ECONOMIC, CULTURAL, SOFTWARE ECOSYSTEM) and a source URL cited for every single data point.
6. AC-6: For AC-2, verify that the artist you selected actually has the country as a tag by checking the tags section on the artist page. If the top result does not have the tag, skip to the next artist that does.

TOTAL EXPECTED PAGES VISITED: >= 45. Do not abbreviate or summarize; every data point must appear individually in the output.
answer_format: Three sections. Section ECONOMIC: table of 6×3 entries (6 countries, 3 indicators) each with country code, indicator name, value, unit, year, and full source URL. Section CULTURAL: table of 6×2 entries (6 countries, 2 artists each) with country, artist name, total listeners, top track name, plays count, and source URL. Section SOFTWARE ECOSYSTEM: header with RubyGems.org total gems and total downloads from /stats (with URL), followed by a table of 5 gems with name, version, downloads, runtime dependency count, and source URL. All values verbatim from the live site.

text:
I'm a graduate student in comparative cultural economics and I need a literature-data annex for my thesis chapter 'The Digital Creative Economy in Five Markets.' Please construct the following evidence table using ONLY publicly visible data from these three sites, and I need every figure traced to its exact source URL.

INSTRUCTION SET:
1. On data.worldbank.org, for each of the five markets — United States, United Kingdom, South Korea, Nigeria, and India — find and record: (a) GDP per capita (current US$), (b) GDP growth rate (annual %), (c) Internet users (% of population), (d) Urban population (% of total population). Navigate to the country-specific indicator pages to get the most recent year's value. That's 20 values.

2. On www.last.fm, I need a 'cultural prominence' proxy. For each market, search the country name, then navigate through tag and artist pages to find exactly 4 artists who: (i) appear in search results for that country, (ii) have a total listener count displayed, and (iii) have at least 3 tracks listed with play counts. For each selected artist record: name, total listeners, top track title, top track play count, and number of top tracks visible on their page. That's 20 artists, 5 fields each = 100 fields.

3. On rubygems.org, I need an 'open-source ecosystem health' baseline. First, from the /stats page, record the total gem count and total download count. Then, from the top section of /stats (the most-downloaded gems list), record the name and download count of the top 10 gems. Then for each of those 10 gems, click into the gem page and record: current version, number of runtime dependencies, and number of authors/maintainers listed. That's 10 gems × 3 fields + 2 aggregate = 32 fields.

4. Cross-reference: Note if any artist name from step 2 also appears as a gem name or in a gem description on rubygems.org (search for the exact artist name on rubygems.org). Record 'MATCH' or 'NO MATCH' for each of the 20 artists.

DELIVERABLE:
A single document with:
- Section 1 header: 'Table A: Macroeconomic Indicators (World Bank)'
  Table: [Market, GDP per Capita (US$), GDP Growth (%), Internet Users (%), Urban Pop (%), All Source URLs, Year(s)]
- Section 2 header: 'Table B: Cultural Prominence Indicators (Last.fm)'
  Table: [Market, Artist Name, Total Listeners, Top Track, Track Plays, Top Tracks Count, Source URL, RubyGems Cross-Ref]
- Section 3 header: 'Table C: Open-Source Ecosystem Baseline (RubyGems.org)'
  Table: [Rank, Gem Name, Downloads, Version, Runtime Deps, Maintainers, Source URL]
- Footer: 'Aggregate baselines — Total gems: N | Total downloads: N | Total data points: N'

Do not use any external sources. If a value is not visible on the page, write 'NOT VISIBLE' rather than guessing.
answer_format: Three labeled tables (A, B, C) plus a footer aggregate line. Table A: 5 rows × ~7 columns. Table B: 20 rows × 8 columns (including cross-ref column). Table C: 10 rows × 7 columns. Footer must state total gems, total downloads, and total data point count. All numeric values must match what is displayed on the live pages at collection time. Source URL required for every row.

text:
I'm a data analyst preparing a weekly briefing on 'entertainment industry legislative attention vs. public interest'. I need you to gather data from three sources and output a normalized table. Here's the procedure:

SOURCE A — https://www.rottentomatoes.com: Go to the 'Best Movies' or top-rated movies section. Take the top 6 movies. For each, I need: title, Tomatometer score (integer, %), Audience Score (integer, %), and the release year if shown. Compute a 'Critic-Audience Gap' column as absolute difference between the two percentages.

SOURCE B — https://www.google.com/travel/flights: Search round-trip LAX → DCA, departing 2026-11-06, returning 2026-11-09. Record: cheapest fare in USD, airline code or name, total outbound duration (in minutes as integer), total return duration (in minutes as integer). Also expand to view the next 3 closest departure dates (2026-11-03, 2026-11-04, 2026-11-05) and for each note the cheapest fare in USD. Present as a small sub-table.

SOURCE C — https://www.congress.gov: Search bills for 'entertainment' restricted to the 119th Congress. Take the first 6 results. For each: bill number, sponsor (last name, first initial), chamber, status keyword (one of: Introduced, Passed House, Passed Senate, Became Law, or Other), and introduction date in YYYY-MM-DD format.

Final deliverable: Three sub-tables clearly labeled, with a summary line stating the average Critic-Audience Gap across the 6 movies, the spread of flight fares across the 4 departure dates (max minus min, in USD), and the number of the 6 bills that have progressed beyond 'Introduced' status. Include the exact source URL used for each site section.
kind: normalized data extraction with computed metrics
answer_format: Three labeled sub-tables (movies with Critic-Audience Gap; flight fares by date with durations in minutes; bills with normalized fields) plus a summary line with three computed values: average gap (%), fare spread (USD), and count of bills past 'Introduced'. Include source URLs per section.

text:

Format the final output as: Part 1 (5-row table), Part 2 (2-row table for flights plus a note on nonstops), Part 3 (table of bills). Add a one-sentence header for each part. No commentary beyond what I asked.
